issue_context.title: series arg_min & arg_max seems inconsistent with min & max
issue_context.body:
### Checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.


### Reproducible example

The following comments about whether it is okay are just my intuition and may not necessarily be correct.

```python
    int_has_null = pl.Series("a", [None, 1], dtype=pl.Int32)
    assert int_has_null.max() == 1 # ok
    assert int_has_null.min() == 1 # ok 
    assert int_has_null.arg_max() == 1 # ok
    assert int_has_null.arg_min() == 0 # weird

    int_all_null = pl.Series("a", [None], dtype=pl.Int32)
    assert int_all_null.max() is None # ok 
    assert int_all_null.min() is None # ok 
    assert int_all_null.arg_max() == 0 # ok
    assert int_all_null.arg_min() == 0 # ok

    boolean_has_null_true = pl.Series("a", [None, True], dtype=pl.Boolean)
    assert boolean_has_null_true.max() is True # ok
    assert boolean_has_null_true.min() is True # ok, maybe.
    assert boolean_has_null_true.arg_max() == 1 # ok
    assert boolean_has_null_true.arg_min() == 0 # weird

    boolean_has_null_false = pl.Series("a", [None, False], dtype=pl.Boolean)
    assert boolean_has_null_false.max() is False # ok
    assert boolean_has_null_false.min() is False # ok
    assert boolean_has_null_false.arg_max() is None # weird
    assert boolean_has_null_false.arg_min() == 0 # weird

    boolean_all_null = pl.Series("a", [None], dtype=pl.Boolean)
    assert boolean_all_null.max() is None # ok
    assert boolean_all_null.min() is None # ok
    assert boolean_all_null.arg_max() == 0 # ok
    assert boolean_all_null.arg_min() == 0 # ok

```


### Issue description

I believe part of the reason is that we did not consider null value when calculating `min` & `max`, but we did consider this when calculating the `arg` counterpart, and we used the comparison rule for `Option<T>` in rust (i.e. `None < Some (_)`).

### Expected behavior

Not very sure which behavior is right(though I tend to the behavior of `min&max`), but at least they should be consistent.

### Installed versions

<details>

Main branch.

</details>
comments: I can submit a PR to keep them consistent, but before that, we need to identify which behavior is what we want. @ritchie46  Any thought about this?
Do you also prefer the way of handling null values in min/max?
I am not sure, but I think `arg_min` should always point to the same value as the `min`.

> `arg_min` should always point to the same value as the min.

Yes, the key point is that we treat `None` as the minimum value for `arg` operation, but not for `non-arg` operation. In theory, modifying either side can ensure that `arg_min` point to the same value as `min`, but if we choose `min` to fit `arg-min`, the following behavior may seem strange to me:

```python
s = pl.Series("a", [None, 1], dtype=pl.Int32)
assert s.min() == None
```

In my intuition, as long as there are `non-null` values in `Series`, neither `min` nor `max` should return `None`.
I think we should modify arg_min to point to the minimal non-null values
So, how I see it, is that `null` values should always (at least by default) be consistently treated as not being there at all unless there is a very good reason otherwise.

> null values should always (at least by default) be consistently treated as not being there at all

IIUC, your suggestion as follows:

```python
    int_all_null = pl.Series("a", [None, None, None], dtype=pl.Int32)
    assert int_all_null.max() is None
    assert int_all_null.min() is None
    assert int_all_null.arg_max() == None
    assert int_all_null.arg_min() == None
```

@reswqa That is correct, my proposal would give the following answers for your test cases above

```rust
    int_has_null = pl.Series("a", [None, 1], dtype=pl.Int32)
    assert int_has_null.max() == 1
    assert int_has_null.min() == 1
    assert int_has_null.arg_max() == 1
    assert int_has_null.arg_min() == 1

    int_all_null = pl.Series("a", [None], dtype=pl.Int32)
    assert int_all_null.max() is None
    assert int_all_null.min() is None
    assert int_all_null.arg_max() == None
    assert int_all_null.arg_min() == None

    boolean_has_null_true = pl.Series("a", [None, True], dtype=pl.Boolean)
    assert boolean_has_null_true.max() is True
    assert boolean_has_null_true.min() is True
    assert boolean_has_null_true.arg_max() == 1
    assert boolean_has_null_true.arg_min() == 1

    boolean_has_null_false = pl.Series("a", [None, False], dtype=pl.Boolean)
    assert boolean_has_null_false.max() is False
    assert boolean_has_null_false.min() is False
    assert boolean_has_null_false.arg_max() == 1
    assert boolean_has_null_false.arg_min() == 1

    boolean_all_null = pl.Series("a", [None], dtype=pl.Boolean)
    assert boolean_all_null.max() is None
    assert boolean_all_null.min() is None
    assert boolean_all_null.arg_max() == None
    assert boolean_all_null.arg_min() == None
```
@orlp I thought for a moment, it seems that this is more reasonable compared to what I previously marked as `ok`, I will open a PR to move in this direction.

review_comments: `None` will always be considered the minimum value as `None < Some(_)`. But I'm not quite sure if it's better to do `flat_map` here or do `match` directly in `reduce`?
Match in reduce will be faster as we have less indirection. I think we should first loop over `downcast_iter` and then loop over the array.

> Match in reduce will be faster as we have less indirection.

 Make sense, will rewrite this.

> I think we should first loop over downcast_iter and then loop over the array.

Does this means rewriting it to the same pattern of `arg_max_numeric` 🤔

They are similar. We could even share a same generic if you are up for that. ^^

But that is maybe a nice follow up PR. :)

I am trying to do this refactoring: Let them both share a same generic function as they are almost similar. The only difference is that for numerical types, we have a fast path with the following bound:

https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/ecb819a6541cbc53bee1bf100d2abc87bb9d0962/crates/polars-ops/src/series/ops/arg_min_max.rs#L248

But for `Utf8ChunkedArray`: we do not have this bound, also we doesn't have this branch:

https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/ecb819a6541cbc53bee1bf100d2abc87bb9d0962/crates/polars-ops/src/series/ops/arg_min_max.rs#L264-L268

I can think of some hack solution (such as a magical macro), but I don't really like that way. Do we have a good solution for this that looks simpler and cleaner 🤔.
Perhaps we can test `ca.null_count() == 0`, and if it doesn't hold up, we can go here. Otherwise, we will still follow the previous logic?
I don't think it would matter much in performance. I leave this up to you.

The previous implementation involved many comparisons of `Options<T>`. It is important to pay great attention to `None < Some(_)`, and for `arg_min`, it will result in unexpected result. I filtered out the `None` value directly here. I'm not very sure if this will have a negative impact, but the previous logic was a bit too complicated.
Can we rewrite this one in `downcast_iter` as well?

Sorry, I didn't quite understand what you meant. Isn't this already in the iteration of `downcast_iter`? I guess it is to rewrite `flap_map` to `match`. If not, could you please explain it in more detail? Thanks!
Oh sorry, my bad. This one is good. :+1:  (missed the context due to github collapsing)
The logic is: we first find `true`, and if it does not exist, we return the first `false` location. Is this exactly what we want?
@reswqa Yes, that's the correct behavior, although I think we can do a faster implementation more explicitly iterating over the bitmap. But that doesn't have to be in this PR.
